title: Generic Identifiability and Directed Containment for Strongly Tree-Child Level-2 Networks under the Kimura Two-Parameter Model: The Principal Positive Domain and Strict Continuous Time
description: An exact, computer-assisted K2P identifiability theorem for strongly tree-child level-two networks, with triangle ambiguity and a sharp weak-class obstruction.
abstract:
We classify regular full-dimensional stochastic containment among binary standard semi-directed strongly tree-child level-2 phylogenetic networks under the Kimura two-parameter (K2P) model. On the principal positive Fourier domain D₊ = {(s, g) : 0 < s < 1, 0 < g < 1, g > 2s − 1}, a directed containment germ exists if and only if the two labelled networks are isomorphic after independently redirecting ordinary three-cycle factors. The same condition is equivalent to a common full-dimensional regular germ; in particular, no proper one-sided containment occurs. It follows that the semi-directed topology is generically identifiable modulo ordinary triangle redirection, and that its structural triangle class is exactly reconstructible away from a proper algebraic exceptional set.

The proof combines pointwise displayed-quartet inequalities and exact whole-map Tᵢ identities, an exact two-sector bridge-fibre theorem, physical marginal submersions, a finite localization argument, and a bounded graph-to-algebra classification of cycle and theta factors. The bounded classification is computer-assisted: every directed primitive relation, rank exclusion, restoration parent, transport, and one-/two-port probe is represented by an exact certificate and has a separately implemented replay and targeted mutation tests. We state this residue explicitly rather than replacing it by an unproved hand-orbit claim. The classification transfers to the strict continuous-time domain 0 < s < 1, s² < g < 1. Finally, for every n ≥ 3 we give two weakly but not strongly tree-child level-2 networks whose continuous-time K2P images share a regular germ of dimension 4n − 3, proving that strong tree-childness is a sharp hypothesis.
plain_language: An evolutionary network can describe events such as hybridization that a family tree cannot. Before trying to reconstruct one from DNA, there is a basic question: could a different network produce exactly the same pattern probabilities?

This paper studies that question for the Kimura two-parameter model, which distinguishes two kinds of DNA substitutions. For a specified class of networks with at most two reticulations in each tangled component, it classifies when one model can reproduce a full-dimensional open piece of another. The remaining structural ambiguity is the direction of an ordinary three-edge cycle.

The qualification about strong tree-childness matters. For every number of taxa from three onward, the paper constructs networks satisfying the weaker tree-child condition that remain indistinguishable on a whole regular region of model outputs. The result concerns exact probability distributions; it is not an analysis of how much real sequence data would be needed.
result: Theorem 7.3 applies to binary standard semi-directed strongly tree-child level-two networks on the same labelled leaf set. Every admissible rooting must be tree-child, and each edge has K2P Fourier spectrum (1, s, g, s) with 0 < s < 1, 0 < g < 1 and g > 2s − 1; inheritance probabilities lie strictly between zero and one. A source-relative regular analytic containment with a physical target section exists exactly when the networks differ only by ordinary triangle redirections. This is also equivalent to sharing a full-dimensional regular germ.

Theorems 8.1 and 9.1 give generic identification and a finite exact reconstruction procedure for that structural triangle class outside a proper algebraic exceptional set. The same classification holds on the strict continuous-time subdomain 0 < s < 1 and s² < g < 1.

Theorem 11.1 supplies the sharpness statement: for every n ≥ 3 there are two nonisomorphic, non-triangle-equivalent level-two networks that are weakly but not strongly tree-child and share a strict continuous-time K2P regular germ of dimension 4n − 3.
why_it_works: Quartet inequalities first recover the tree of network components. Exact identities, positive bridge factorizations and physical marginal maps reduce a proposed global containment to comparisons of bounded local factors.

A finite computer-assisted classification then examines the directed local possibilities, including restored attachments and probes that recover the order of arbitrary subdivisions. Explicit triangle germs and compatible bridge gluing establish the converse. The exact certificates and separately implemented checkers are part of the proof; the manuscript does not replace that computation with a short handwritten classification.
limitations: The theorem uses the stated binary, simple, standard semi-directed convention, level at most two, strong tree-childness, a uniform root distribution and independent inheritance choices. It does not cover arbitrary phylogenetic networks, the multispecies coalescent model or unrestricted substitution models.

All edge and inheritance inequalities are strict. Zero or boundary parameters, mixed-sign Fourier spectra and arbitrary stochastic K2P parameters outside the principal positive domain are outside the theorem.
Triangle equivalence is a structural ambiguity. A shared regular germ is not a claim that the entire physical model images are equal, and the theorem does not identify all numerical parameters.

Reconstruction assumes exact distributions and effective exact arithmetic, sign decisions and real-closed-field quantifier elimination. The O(n⁹) statement counts bounded leaf restrictions after input preparation; it is not a polynomial-time or bit-complexity guarantee. No finite-sample accuracy or numerical conditioning guarantee is proved.

The bounded classification remains a load-bearing exact computation. Archived verification summaries alone do not establish its correctness. This page describes an unrefereed preprint, not an independent human peer review.

background.title: Englander et al. — Identifiability of phylogenetic level-2 networks under the Jukes–Cantor model
background.note: The July 2026 version 4 supplies the JC/K2P displayed-quartet inequalities and tree-of-blobs separation used here; its main level-two algebraic classification is for JC.

background.title: Huber et al. — When are quarnets sufficient to reconstruct semi-directed phylogenetic networks?
background.note: Lemma 4.2 and Figure 8 give the two semi-directed level-two generator types. The present paper adds directed port and attachment information for its classification.

background.title: Brits et al. — On tree–network distinguishability and full identifiability of phylogenetic networks
background.note: Theorem 4.9 gives the preceding level-one JC/K2P/K3P identifiability result modulo triangle placement on its positive parameter domain.

background.title: Holtgrefe et al. — Characterizing semi-directed phylogenetic networks and their multi-rootable variants
background.note: Background for rooting, strong and weak tree-childness, and the no-omnian criterion; the manuscript fixes its own precise binary suppression convention.
